label: Online fatigue
summary: Online fatigue is the exhaustion that builds up during online meetings. It is commonly attributed to communication gaps like missing body language and cultural friction, but Maaike points to postural collapse as an underappreciated physical cause. The two reinforce each other: the more tired you get, the more you sink in on yourself, and the more collapsed your posture, the worse you feel.
how_maaike_uses: Maaike uses online fatigue as a hook to bring embodied awareness into a conversation that usually stays at the level of technology or organisational culture. Her angle is practical and body-first: she argues that noticing your sitting bones, feet on the floor, and the tendency of your head to drift toward the screen gives you a way to interrupt the collapse before it becomes total. The tips she offers are not about effort or holding yourself rigid, but about redirecting attention to physical sensations that are already there.
open_questions: The post mentions that sloppy posture and fatigue reinforce each other in a downward spiral, but it does not say how much postural work alone can compensate when the meeting culture or communication problems are the main driver.
It is left open whether these embodied strategies help equally for people with chronic fatigue or physical conditions that make an upright posture harder to sustain.
